Keep the original stack rule unchanged after the contract changes; only the final output formatting needs to be updated.
Any sequential problem that refers to previous or future elements still requires some form of stack, regardless of updates or query semantics.

feedback.reason: Entries no longer mean unmatched openers; they become unresolved `(priority,index)` candidates maintained by a strict comparison rule.

blocks.text: Nested validation retains typed unmatched openers and pops one compatible top on closure. The new output ignores closure and gives every index a nearest strictly greater right answer; retain `(priority,index)`, pop smaller tops when current first qualifies, and keep a non-increasing frontier. Keeping the old rule would answer nesting instead of priority, while the token domain itself selects neither algorithm.

feedback.reason: Yes. A new warmer value permanently finalizes the nearest-right answer of every smaller unresolved top; no future edit can invalidate it.

On each append, pop every smaller top and emit `currentIndex - oldIndex`; append order proves current is the first qualifying later value, so that answer is final. Push current afterward. The algorithm needs no future random access, but days never resolved must remain pending until stream completion or an explicit finalization event.

items.prompt: An array supports arbitrary point updates and online nearest-greater queries. After computing answers for `[5,1,4]`, value `5` may be updated to `0`. Can the old one-pass frontier always be repaired locally?

options.text: The stack can be patched locally after any update.
Keep the original stack rule unchanged after the contract changes; only the final output formatting needs to be updated.
Any sequential problem that refers to previous or future elements still requires some form of stack, regardless of updates or query semantics.
Previously finalized dominance relations can become invalid after mutation.

feedback.reason: No. Updating `5` to `0` changes earlier dominance and nearest answers beyond the edited stack suffix; the irreversible one-pass proof no longer applies.

blocks.text: A one-pass frontier safely discards candidates only because processed values never change. In `[5,1,4]`, `5` blocks relations that differ after it becomes `0`; queries for several positions can change, and discarded candidates cannot be reconstructed from the old frontier. Local repair is not generally proved. Rebuild for infrequent updates or choose a dynamic indexed structure whose update/query contract is explicit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: An arbitrary edit can affect many previously finalized relationships, not only entries adjacent to the changed position.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: The old maintenance rule assumes immutable processed input and is invalid under the new update model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: A dynamic problem may require a segment tree or rebuild strategy rather than any stack.

items.prompt: The same sequence must support many repeated queries and may also receive updates. Select all alternatives that can be preferable to rebuilding one monotonic stack per query.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.

options.text: Arbitrary updates can always be repaired locally in the old stack without invalidating finalized relationships.
Static prefix or suffix preprocessing when the repeated query has a compatible one-way aggregate.
A segment tree or related indexed structure when point updates and range queries must both be supported.
An offline sorted or sweep-based method when all queries are known in advance and global ordering is useful.
A one-pass monotonic stack is always asymptotically optimal regardless of query volume or updates.

feedback.reason: Static repetition, dynamic updates, and offline batches expose different reusable work, so they can justify preprocessing, indexed trees, or sorted sweeps instead of per-query rebuilds.

blocks.text: For immutable compatible aggregates, one prefix/suffix build can answer many queries cheaply. With point updates plus range queries, a segment tree pays logarithmic maintenance rather than rebuilding O(n) state. When all queries are known, sorting or a sweep may share global work across them. None is universally best; the accepted options are conditional alternatives. The two false claims ignore either repeated O(n) rebuild cost or mutation of finalized relations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: A one-pass O(n) method per query can be worse than one reusable preprocessing build or dynamic index.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: Arbitrary updates can invalidate many old relations and have no general local-stack repair proof.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: It reuses work when the data is static and the query is a compatible directional aggregate.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: It directly supports the stated combination of updates and range queries.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: It exploits known-in-advance queries and global order that an online stack cannot share.

feedback.reason: Use structural scope state plus a scope-owned monotonic frontier; close events and greater-value resolution have different triggers and lifetimes.

blocks.text: The scope stack pushes on open and pops on the matching close. The active scope’s monotonic frontier pops smaller measurements when current resolves them; closing the scope assigns no-answer to its survivors and restores the parent frontier. One implicit hybrid predicate could let a comparison close a scope or let a close discard another scope’s candidates. Separate ownership makes both invariants explicit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: One stack entry cannot safely obey both structural-close and comparison-pop semantics without explicit role separation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: The new within-scope output adds state and lifecycle requirements, not just formatting.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Here two stack-shaped roles are justified by separate contracts; sequentiality alone would not be enough.

blocks.text: The work stack schedules pending DFS frames in LIFO order. Along the current root-to-node path, a separate frontier removes dominated ancestors and exposes the nearest greater ancestor. Every change to that frontier must be recorded and rolled back on exit so siblings see only their own ancestors. A global unrolled frontier leaks candidates across sibling paths; sharing one invariant confuses scheduling with comparison.

Pushing current then preserves non-increasing values. An increasing frontier would not expose the smaller resolvable suffix, and calling the order strictly decreasing would mishandle duplicates.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Increasing order exposes the wrong suffix for a larger-current resolver.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: The frontier must be derived from strict comparison and duplicates, not retained from another contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: This contract admits a stack because answers finalize in one scan; not every future-reference task does.

items.prompt: Select all contracts for which no stack is the primary justified structure.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: Answer range-maximum queries while point updates are allowed.
Support random deletion by identity together with global rank queries.
Undo the most recent command in reverse chronological order.
Resolve next-greater candidates with one-way safe deletion during a fixed scan.
Maintain a dynamic median under arbitrary insertions and deletions.

feedback.reason: Dynamic median, mutable range maximum, and random deletion with rank queries need updateable global/indexed order rather than LIFO or irreversible one-way deletion.

blocks.text: A dynamic median needs balanced ordered multisets or heaps with deletion support. Point-update range maximum fits a segment tree or related index. Random deletion plus rank queries needs an order-statistics structure. Undo is exactly LIFO, and fixed-scan next greater is exactly one-way safe candidate deletion, so those two false options do justify stacks. Input arrival order alone cannot override the update/query contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: Reverse chronological Undo is the canonical ordinary LIFO contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: Fixed one-way next-greater finalization is the canonical monotonic-stack contract.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: Arbitrary median maintenance needs global order under insertions and deletions.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: Point updates can invalidate many static boundaries, while an indexed tree maintains range aggregates.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: Random identity deletion and ranks conflict with top-only access and require order statistics.

items.prompt: A next-greater routine deletes `2` when its nearest greater value `3` arrives. The output changes to list every greater pair. Does the deletion remain safe for `[2,3,4]`?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Keep the original stack rule unchanged after the contract changes; only the final output formatting needs to be updated.
Any sequential problem that refers to previous or future elements still requires some form of stack, regardless of updates or query semantics.
Replacing nearest qualifying answer with all qualifying pairs or a future optimum removes finality at pop time.
The algorithm remains valid under any broader output.

feedback.reason: No. After deleting `2` at `3`, the routine cannot later emit required pair `(2,4)`; pop-time finality depended on nearestness.

blocks.text: Nearest output for `2` is finalized at `3`, so forgetting `2` is safe. All-pairs output for `[2,3,4]` requires `(2,3)`, `(2,4)`, and `(3,4)`. The old state loses `2` before `4`, making `(2,4)` unrecoverable. A broader output can invalidate deletion even when input, comparison word, and loop shape are unchanged.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: `(2,4)` is a concrete required output the unchanged algorithm cannot produce.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: Changing only formatting cannot recover candidate `2` after the old rule deletes it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: The broader sequential output may require another method because the old stack’s safe-deletion proof has failed.

State the original output and the semantic meaning of one retained entry.
Name the smallest material change, such as structural closure becoming nearest qualifying boundary.
Derive how the retained entry changes from pending recent state to ordered unresolved candidate, or the reverse.
State the new invariant and exact pop trigger required by that entry meaning.

feedback.reason: A valid transfer argument starts from output, identifies the material change, then derives entry meaning, invariant, pop trigger, and correctness.

items: State the original delimiter-validity output and unmatched-opener entry meaning.
Name the material change to nearest later strictly greater priority.
Derive the new unresolved `(priority,index)` candidate meaning.
State the non-increasing frontier and `current > top` pop trigger.
Use scan order to prove that each pop finalizes the nearest answer.

blocks.text: Reversing the transfer requires the same chain in reverse; a label cannot change without a material contract change.
